title: From Caravans to Containers
objective: After this level you can trace how trade routes grew from the Silk Road to container ships.
summary: The Silk Road linked China and the West, with goods passed along by middlemen. In 1956, Malcolm McLean's containers made loading ships far cheaper than handling loose cargo.

cards.headline: Silk crossed Asia for centuries, yet almost nobody made the whole trip.
cards.body: On the Silk Road, few people traveled the entire route. Goods moved in stages, handed from middleman to middleman. This level follows how goods traveled, from camel caravans to steel boxes.

cards.headline: The Silk Road
cards.body: The Silk Road was a caravan route of about 6,400 km linking China with the West, carrying goods and ideas between China and Rome. Silk went west; wool, gold and silver went east. Religions traveled it too, and so did diseases. After years as an unsafe, little-used route, it revived under the Mongols. That's when Marco Polo went east, and came home describing Level 5's Chinese paper money.

cards.headline: One sack at a time
cards.body: Ships carried goods much farther than camels, but loading them stayed slow. Sacks, barrels and crates were handled one by one. This loose, break-bulk cargo could take several days to load, so ships often sat in port for long periods. Picture packing for a house move one sock at a time.

mascot.line: All that way across the ocean, and the slowest part was the dock.

cards.fact: April 26, 1956: 58 boxes set sail, and loading got cheap.
cards.context: Trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent his ship, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal containers. Instead of loose cargo, whole boxes went aboard. Loading a ship the conventional way cost more than $5.80 a ton. Loading McLean's containers cost about 16 cents.

cards.headline: Caravans to containers
learned: The Silk Road linked China and the West
Goods passed along it through middlemen
Loose cargo made loading ships slow
McLean's 1956 containers made loading far cheaper

questions.prompt: How did goods usually travel the length of the Silk Road?

options.label: One merchant carried them all the way
options.rationale: Few people made the whole journey.

options.label: They passed in stages between middlemen
Roman convoys escorted them end to end
options.rationale: The route was a caravan tract worked by middlemen, not convoys.

options.label: They went by container ship
options.rationale: Containers came many centuries later, in 1956.

questions.explanation: Few people traveled the whole route; goods moved along it in stages through middlemen.

questions.prompt: Why did McLean's containers make loading ships so much cheaper?

options.label: Whole boxes went aboard instead of loose cargo
The ships were much smaller
options.rationale: Size wasn't the point; the loading method was.

options.label: Dockworkers were no longer paid
options.rationale: Loading still took work; it just took far less.

options.label: The goods inside weighed less
options.rationale: The cargo was the same kind of goods, packed differently.

questions.explanation: Loading whole containers replaced handling sacks, barrels and crates one by one, cutting the cost from more than $5.80 a ton to about 16 cents.

questions.prompt: Marco Polo traveled the revived Silk Road. From Level 5, what Chinese money did he describe for Europeans?

options.label: Cowrie shells
options.rationale: Cowries were early money, but Polo is remembered for describing paper money.

options.label: Gold coins stamped with a lion
options.rationale: Lion-stamped coins were Lydia's, from Level 4.

options.label: Stone discs
options.rationale: Stone discs were Yap's money, from Level 3.

questions.explanation: Marco Polo gave one of the earliest European accounts of China's paper money.
